parole.significato: Used in combination with prefixes to form imperfective verbs with an approximate meaning “to clothe, to dress, to put o…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dęgati, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ-, *dʰn̥gʰ- (“to cover, conceal”). By surface analysis, дягти (djahty) + -а́ти (-áty). Cognate with Lithuanian deñgti (“to cover, to dress”).

parole.significato: Used in combination with prefixes to form perfective verbs with an approximate meaning “to clothe, to dress, to put on”.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dęgnǫti, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ-, *dʰn̥gʰ- (“to cover, conceal”). Cognate with Lithuanian deñgti (“to cover, to dress”).

parole.significato: Used in combination with prefixes to form perfective verbs with an approximate meaning “to clothe, to dress, to put on”.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dęťi, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ-, *dʰn̥gʰ- (“to cover, conceal”). Cognate with Lithuanian deñgti (“to cover, to dress”).

parole.significato: Only used in conjunction with prefixes to form perfective verbs with an approximate meaning "to pull (together), to lin…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mъknǫti.

parole.significato: Suffix added to nouns and adjectives to create an abstract noun, corresponding to English -ness, -hood, -dom.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьstvo, from Proto-Indo-European *-tus.

parole.significato: Forms verbs from nouns and adjectives, as well as loanwords.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ovati. Compare Macedonian -ува (-uva), Polish -ować.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьce, from Proto-Indo-European *-ikos.

parole.significato: Suffix appended to imperfective verbs to create a masculine noun denoting action.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-otъ.
From Proto-Slavic *(j)ešče (“still, yet”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁esk(ʷ)e(h₁). Cognate with Russian ещё (ješčó).
Inherited from Old East Slavic агньць (agnĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *agnьcь, a derivative of *àgnę; eventually from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷnós.

parole.significato: leader at any activities (parties, choir, caroling etc.)
parole.testo: From older form *березий (*berezyj, “striped, white with black”), from Proto-Slavic *berzъ, which is related to Bulgarian бряз (brjaz). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *blizъ.

parole.significato: to take, to grab; but while брати is generic, дістати means "to take out (from, e.g. the fridge or a box)" and it is fo…
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic бьрати (bĭrati), from Proto-Slavic *bьrati. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.
From Proto-Slavic *brexati, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerk-, from *bʰer-. Cognate with Belarusian брахаць (braxacʹ), Russian брехать (brexatʹ), Slovak brechat'.
From Proto-Slavic *brexati, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerk-, from *bʰer-. Cognate with Belarusian брахаць (braxacʹ), Russian брехать (brexatʹ), Slovak brechat'.
Inherited from Old East Slavic бродити (broditi), from Proto-Slavic *brodìti, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrodʰ-eye-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰredʰ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bojь, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoyh₂ós, from *bʰeyh₂- (“to strike, hew”).

parole.significato: in, at [with locative] (used to express static position/location; followed by a vowel)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic въ (vŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vъ(n), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥, zero-grade form of *h₁én.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vę̄zàti.
From Proto-Slavic *variti, from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to burn”).

parole.significato: your, yours (2nd-person singular formal or 2nd-person plural)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *vašь, from Proto-Indo-European *wōsyo-.

parole.significato: to hit, to strike, to smite (to deal a blow)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian уда́рити, вда́рити (udáriti, vdáriti), from Old East Slavic оударити (udariti), from Proto-Slavic *udariti, from Proto-Indo-European *derH-.

parole.significato: one of the ropes on which a baby cradle is suspended
parole.testo: Derived from Old East Slavic вьрвь (vĭrvĭ), from Proto-Slavic *vьrvь (deverbal of *verti), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to tie, string; rope”) which is ultimately cognate with *wer- (“to turn, bend”) whence the two meanings of the verb. Compare Russian верёвка (verjóvka), whence Ukrainian вірьо́
From Proto-Slavic *večerъ, from Proto-Indo-European *wekʷsperos.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian ви́дѣти (víděti), from Old East Slavic видѣти (viděti), from Proto-Slavic *viděti, from Proto-Indo-European *weyd-. Cognate with Bulgarian ви́дя (vídja), Latin videō, English wit, wise, Russian ви́деть (vídetʹ).
From Proto-Slavic *vitati, from Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁- (“to chase, pursue”). Doublet of віта́ти (vitáty, “greet”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vorxъ. Cognate with Russian во́рох (vórox, “heap, pile”), Belarusian во́рох (vórox, “noise”), Bulgarian врах (vrah, “sheaves intended for threshing”), Polish zawroch (“blizzard, whirlwind”). More distantly cognate with Russian Church Slavonic врѣшти (vrěšti, “to hammer”)
Inherited from Old Ruthenian во́инъ (vóin), from Old East Slavic воинъ (voinŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vojinъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁-.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian о́смъ (ósm). From Proto-Slavic *osmь, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *usta.

From Proto-Slavic *uxo, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ous-. Compare Russian у́хо (úxo) and Belarusian ву́ха (vúxa). Cognate with Old Armenian ունկն (unkn), Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐍃𐍉 (ausō), Ancient Greek οὖς (oûs), Latin auris, Modern Persian گوش (guš).
From Proto-Slavic *ovьca, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃éwis. With -я (-ja).
From Proto-Slavic *vozъ, from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-.
From Proto-Slavic *vьjь, *vijь (“bundle of twigs”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyǵh- (“to twist, weave”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *olьxa, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éliseh₂, from *h₂élis-. Cognate with Belarusian во́льха (vólʹxa), Bulgarian елха́ (elhá), Polish olcha.
From Proto-Slavic *onъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énos (“that”).

Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣникъ (věnikŭ), from Proto-Slavic *věnikъ, from *věnъ (“wreath”) + *-ikъ, details of further origin unclear (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *woh₁y-nos or derived later) but ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁y- (“to twist, wind, weave”). Related to віне́ць (v

parole.significato: a vinok, a wreath traditionally worn by women.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic вѣнъкъ (věnŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *věnъkъ, from *věnъ (“wreath”) + *-ъkъ, details of further origin unclear (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wóh₁y-nós or derived later) but ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁y- (“to twist, wind, weave”).
From Proto-Slavic *větvь, *větь, from Proto-Indo-European *wéh₁itis.
Possibly related to Proto-Slavic *věďa (“eyelid”), or *věja (“tree branch”) (from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁y- (“to bend, twist, turn”)).

parole.significato: to rot, to putrefy, to go bad, to decay, to decompose
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gňiti.
From Proto-Slavic *golъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gelH- (“naked, bald”).

parole.significato: walnut tree, especially common walnut (Juglans regia)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic орѣхъ (orěxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *orěxъ, from Proto-Indo-European *areyis-.
From Middle Ukrainian играти (yhraty), from Old East Slavic играти (igrati), from Proto-Slavic *jьgrati. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyg-.

parole.significato: to thunder (to make a noise like thunder)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic грьмѣти (grĭměti), from Proto-Slavic *grьměti, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrem-.
From Old East Slavic грѫдь (grǫdĭ), from Proto-Slavic *grǫdь, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰrendʰ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *grěnъka, *grěnъkъ, from Proto-Slavic *grěti (“to heat”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“warm”).

parole.significato: to give off warmth, to give off heat
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *grěti, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“warm”).
From Proto-Slavic *gǫ̑sь, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns.

parole.significato: door, doors (portal of entry into a building or room)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *dvьrь, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer-.
From Proto-Slavic *devętь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥.
From Proto-Slavic *devętь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥.

From Old East Slavic деревѧнꙑи (derevęnyi), from Proto-Slavic *dervěnъ, from Proto-Indo-European *derwēno- / *derwoyno-, from *deru- (see *dóru). Morphologically *dervo (“tree”) + *-ěnъ. Equivalent to де́рево (dérevo) + -я́ний (-jányj). Compare Russian деревя́нный (derevjánnyj), Belarusian драўля́ны
From Proto-Slavic *dervo, from Proto-Indo-European *dóru. Doublet of дре́во (drévo).

From Old Ruthenian дзвони́ти (dzvoníti), from Old East Slavic звонити (zvoniti), from Proto-Slavic *zvoniti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwen-. Cognates with Polish dzwonić, Serbo-Croatian зво̀нити.

parole.significato: to, toward (it can indicate a general direction, instead of the final destination of the movement; see на)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian до (do), from Old East Slavic до (do), from Proto-Slavic *do, from Proto-Indo-European *de, *do.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dorga.

parole.significato: to nap, to have a nap, to doze, to slumber, to drowse
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drěmati, from Proto-Indo-European *drēm-ye-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”).

parole.significato: oak (tree of the genus Quercus and its wood)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *dǫbъ, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰanw-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *děva.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian жаръ (žar), from Old East Slavic жаръ (žarŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žārъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰēr- (“heat”, root noun), from *gʷʰer- (“heat, hot”), whence also Proto-Slavic *gorěti, whence Ukrainian горі́ти (horíty, “to burn”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žerbę, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrebʰ-. Cognate with Belarusian жарабя́ (žarabjá), Old Church Slavonic жрѣбѧ (žrěbę), Polish źrebię.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žerbьcь, from *žerbę, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrebʰ-. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic жрѣбѧ (žrěbę), Bulgarian жребе́ц (žrebéc), Polish źrebiec (“colt”). Compare Ancient Greek βρέφος (bréphos, “baby, foetus”).
From Proto-Slavic *živъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”).

parole.significato: to chew, to masticate, to munch
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьvati (“to chew”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁-.

parole.significato: from (from inside a place, e.g., a building or a geographical place)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *jьz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs.

parole.significato: with (somebody, with a comitative meaning; otherwise, to express "with/using/through something" with an instrumental me…
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *sъ(n), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱom.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian зва́ти (zváti), from Old East Slavic зъвати (zŭvati), from Proto-Slavic *zъvati, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewH-.
Variant of зрі́ти (zríty). From Old East Slavic зьрѣти (zĭrěti, “to see, to ripen”), from Proto-Slavic *zьrěti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₁-.
From Proto-Slavic *zьrno, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm.

From Middle Ukrainian знати (znaty), from Old East Slavic знати (znati), from Proto-Slavic *znati, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-. Cognate with Carpathian Rusyn зна́ти (znáty), Russian знать (znatʹ), Belarusian знаць (znacʹ), etc.
From Proto-Slavic *sъ(n), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱom.
Inherited from Old East Slavic золото (zoloto), from Proto-Slavic *zolto, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰolh₃tom (o-grade), from *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”).
From Old East Slavic зьрѣти (zĭrěti, “to ripen”), from Proto-Slavic *zьrěti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵerh₂-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zętь, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁-.
From Old East Slavic казати (kazati), from Proto-Slavic *kazati. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeǵ-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kakati. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kakka-. Compare Serbo-Croatian kakati, kakiti, Italian cacare.

Derived from the same root as кипі́ти (kypíty, “to boil”), from Proto-Slavic *kypě̀ti, from Proto-Indo-European *kwep-, whence English covet and hope. Compare Russian кипяти́ть (kipjatítʹ), Belarusian кіпяці́ць (kipjacícʹ).

parole.significato: to boil, to simmer, to seethe
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *kypě̀ti, from Proto-Indo-European *kwep-, whence English cupidity, covet and hope.

parole.significato: to put, to place, to lay
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klasti, from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂-.
From Old East Slavic колєсѣ (kolesě), the dual number of коло (kolo), from Proto-Slavic *kolo, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷekʷlom (“circle”), *kʷékʷlos (“circle”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *komaxa. Morphologically, most likely from the onomatopoeic root Proto-Indo-European *komH- (“to hum”) + -аха (-axa).
From Proto-Slavic *kopyto, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoph₂ós.
From Old East Slavic кора (kora, “bark”), from Proto-Slavic *kora (“bark”), from Proto-Indo-European *ker-.

parole.significato: to jag, to shred, to hack
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *krem- + *-sati, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krem-, from *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Compare Russian кромса́ть (kromsátʹ).

parole.significato: disc (UK), disk (US) (region of a plane bounded by a circle)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫda.

Related to Old East Slavic кꙋчма (kučma), Russian ку́чма (kúčma), Belarusian ку́чма (kúčma), Polish kuczma, Czech kučma, Slovak kučma, Serbo-Croatian ку̑чма / kȗčma, Slovene kúčma, Bulgarian ку́чма (kúčma), кушма́ (kušmá), and probably inherited from Proto-Slavic *kučьma, which is related to Proto-S
From Proto-Slavic *olbǫdь, from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós (“white”).
From Old East Slavic летѣти (letěti), from Proto-Slavic *letěti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lēk- (“to hop”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lъža, from *lъgati + *-ja; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- and *-yeh₂. Compare Bulgarian лъжа́ (lăžá).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *listъ (“leaf”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lovъ.

parole.significato: man, person, human being, singular of люди (ljudy) (a people, folk, mankind, men)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *ľudina, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“men, people”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lěxa (“furrow, bed”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lóyseh₂ (“furrow”). The unexpected initial ля- (instead of the regular development лі-) is possibly due to the influence of the semantically related ля́да (ljáda, “plot of land, clearing”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lěsъ (“tree, forest”).
From Proto-Slavic *lěto (“summer”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁tom.
From Proto-Slavic *męso, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗms.
From Old East Slavic макъ (makŭ, “poppy; poppy seeds; poppy seed”), from Proto-Slavic *makъ (“poppy”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂kos.

A nursery word. From Proto-Slavic *mama, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-méh₂, a reduplication of *meh₂- - the root of *méh₂tēr (“mother”). Cognate with German Muhme (“aunt”), Latin mamma (“mother, nurse”), Irish mam (“mother”), Lithuanian mama, moma (“mother”) among others. Cf. Proto-Slavic *tata, *
From Old East Slavic мати (mati), from Proto-Slavic *mati, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.
From Proto-Slavic *mьňьjь + -ше (-še), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“small, little”), whence English minor.
From Proto-Slavic *mьrtvъ, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, *mr̥tós, ultimately from the root *mr̥-, *mer- (“to die”).
From Proto-Slavic *myšь, from Proto-Indo-European *muh₂s. The computing term is a semantic loan from English mouse.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *moťi, from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ-. Cognate with Belarusian магчы́ (mahčý), Bulgarian мо́га (móga), Serbo-Croatian мо̏ћи, Czech moci, English may, Dutch mogen, Icelandic mega.
From Proto-Slavic *mozgъ, from Proto-Indo-European *mosgʰós.
From Proto-Slavic *moltъ, from Proto-Indo-European *molh₂-to-, from *melh₂-.
From Old East Slavic море (more), from Proto-Slavic *moře, from Proto-Indo-European *móri.
From Proto-Slavic *mořakъ (by surface analysis, мо́ре (móre, “sea”) + -я́к (-ják)), from Proto-Slavic *moře, from Proto-Indo-European *móri, whence English marine and maritime.
From Proto-Slavic *morvъ, from Proto-Indo-European *morwi- + -аха (-axa).
From Proto-Slavic *měsęcь, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s.
From Proto-Slavic *naviděti, from *viděti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyd-. Cognate with Czech náviděti, Polish nawidzieć.

parole.significato: to attract, to draw, to entice, to tempt, to allure
parole.testo: Most likely from Proto-Slavic *na (“on”) + Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put”), with the semantic shift: to put on → to hook, to bait (fish) → to attract, to allure. Compare a nearly identical formation: наді́ти (nadíty).
Inherited from Old East Slavic нꙑнѣ (nyně), from Proto-Slavic *nyně, from Proto-Indo-European *nu (“now”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *niščь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *nòvъ, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos, with -ий (-yj).

From Proto-Slavic *ňaňa, a reduplicated nursery formation. Similar nursery formations are widespread in Proto-Indo-European; compare Sanskrit नना (nanā́, “mother”), Ancient Greek νάννα (nánna, “aunt”), Albanian nënë (“mother”), Welsh nain (“grandmother”).
From Proto-Slavic *ni, from Proto-Indo-European *néy.
From Proto-Slavic *nosъ, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s.

parole.significato: prefix added to adjectives or nouns to produce factitive verbs in conjunction with -ити (-iti), i.e. verbs with the mea…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *o(b), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ebʰi.
From Proto-Slavic *osa, from Proto-Indo-European *wobʰseh₂.
From Old East Slavic отьць (otĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *otьcь, from Proto-Indo-European *átta.
From Old East Slavic паукъ (paukŭ), from Proto-Slavic *paǫkъ, from *pa- + *ǫkъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enkos (“hook”).

parole.significato: to move, to trudge, to drag the feet
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *perti, from Proto-Indo-European *préy, whence English fare and ferry as well as German fahren.
Proto-Slavic *pьrvь and *pьrvě, from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥Hwós, from *pr̥H- (the root for "before" and "first"). Cognate with Russian прежде (prežde) and Belarusian перш (pjerš).
From Old East Slavic пиво (pivo, “drink, beverage; beer”), from Proto-Slavic *pivo (“drink, beverage; beer”), from Proto-Indo-European *ph₃iwom.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ploskъ. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“thin, flat”). Doublet of пласки́й (plaskýj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *poľe.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *poltьno, from Proto-Indo-European *polto- (“cloth”), from Proto-Indo-European *pel-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pra-.
From Old East Slavic мати (mati), from Proto-Slavic *mati, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. By surface analysis, пра- (pra-) + мати (maty).
From Old East Slavic мати (mati), from Proto-Slavic *mati, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. By surface analysis, пра- (pra-) + мати (maty) + -ір (-ir)
Inherited from Old Ruthenian пѣхо́та, пехо́та (pěxóta, pexóta), from Proto-Slavic *pěxota, which is derived from Proto-Indo-European *pēd-, a variant of *ped-.

parole.significato: foot (attributive), pedestrian (of or for people who walk)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *pěšь. Ultimately a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *pṓds.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *radǫga. The first element more likely derives from Proto-Slavic *radъ than folk etymology’s Proto-Slavic *rajь. The second element from Proto-Slavic *dǫga would be cognate with Lithuanian dangùs (“sky, heaven”) and perhaps further Proto-Germanic *tunglą (“heavenly body”)
From Proto-Slavic *ordlo, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érh₃trom.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *orsti.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian румꙗный (rumjanyj), Proto-Slavic *ruměnъ, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-.

From Ukrainian рух (rux, “movement”) from Old East Slavic рꙋшити (rušiti) from Proto-Slavic *ruxъ from Proto-Indo-European *reu̯, or *rou̯, or *rū. Cognate with Lithuanian ruošа̀ (“preparation”), Lithuanian ruõšti (“to prepare, to equip”), Latvian rа̄oss (“active, eager”), Latin ruō (“to hurry, hast
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rębъ (“speckled, spotted”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁erbʰ-, see also Ancient Greek ὀρφνός (orphnós, “dark brown”).

parole.significato: to scold, to tell off, to admonish, to chide, to rip into
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian свари́ти (svaríti), from Old East Slavic свари́ти (svaríti), from Proto-Slavic *svariti, from Proto-Indo-European *swer-. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic сварити (svariti), Polish swarzyć, English swear.

parole.significato: one's, my, his, her, its, our, your, their (always refers to the subject of the sentence)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *svojь, from Proto-Indo-European *swoyos.

parole.significato: Serb, Serbian (male person from Serbia or of Serbian ethnicity)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sьrbъ.

parole.significato: to yank, to tug, to jerk
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *smykati.
From Proto-Slavic *sněgъ, from Proto-Indo-European *snóygʷʰos.
From Proto-Slavic *solma, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱolh₂mos.
From Proto-Slavic *sъ̀nъ, from Proto-Indo-European *supnós.
From Old East Slavic сълньце (sŭlnĭce), from Proto-Slavic *sъlnьce, from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥.

parole.significato: lentil (any of several plants of the genus Lens, especially Lens culinaris, from southwest Asia, that have edible, lens…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic сочевица (sočevica), from Proto-Slavic *sočevica and *sočivo, probably from *sòkъ (“juice”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷos. Compare Russian чечеви́ца (čečevíca), Belarusian сачаві́ца (sačavíca), Polish soczewica.

Inherited from Old East Slavic спѣти (spěti, “to succede, to hurry, to strive for, to facilitate”), from Proto-Slavic *spěti, from Proto-Indo-European *spewd- (“press, hurry”). Cognate with Bulgarian успе́я (uspéja), Old Church Slavonic спѣти (spěti), Slovene speti, Slovak spieť, Czech spět. Non-Sla
From Proto-Slavic *stopa, from Proto-Indo-European *stebʰ- (“to stand still”). See also Russian стопа́ (stopá), Polish stopa; akin to Lithuanian stapytis.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *strěla.
From Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti, from Proto-Indo-European *stab- (“to support”). Compare Russian ступи́ть (stupítʹ), Belarusian ступі́ць (stupícʹ), Polish stąpnąć.
From Proto-Slavic *sedmь, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.

From Proto-Slavic *solь, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *sḗh₂l. Cognates include Russian соль (solʹ), Polish sól, Sanskrit सलिल (salila), Ancient Greek ἅλς (háls), Armenian աղ (aġ), Latin sāl, and Old English sealt (English salt).
From Proto-Slavic *sedmь, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.

parole.significato: a town that was part of the greater sich (Січ)
parole.testo: Deverbal from сі́кти (síkty), from Proto-Slavic *sěťi, from Proto-Indo-European *sek-.

Inherited from Old East Slavic сѣчень (sěčenĭ), from Proto-Slavic *sěčьňь (“January, February”), lit. "the month of tree cutting", from Proto-Slavic *sěťi (“to cut”), from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”), with -ень (-enʹ). Cognates include Polish styczeń (“January”), Serbo-Croatian siječanj (“J
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tesla / *teslo (“adze”), from Proto-Indo-European *tetḱ-dʰlo-, from *tetḱ-.

parole.significato: to quake, to quiver, to shake, to shiver, to tremble
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trьmtěti, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *trem-.
From Proto-Slavic *trьje, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *trupъ (“(tree) stump”), with this meaning still present in Czech and Polish trup, from Proto-Indo-European *truH-p. Perhaps related to Lithuanian traupus (“fragile,brittle”), Greek τρυπώ (trupṓ, “bore”). Compare Russian труп (trup), Belarusian труп (trup), Bulgarian труп

parole.significato: dark cloud, heavy cloud, rain cloud
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic туча (tuča), from Proto-Slavic *tǫča, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tenk- (“to contract”). Compare the Slavic Old Church Slavonic тѫча (tǫča), Russian ту́ча (túča), Polish tęcza and the Non-Slavic Gothic 𐌸𐌴𐌹𐍈𐍉𐌽 (þeiƕōn) and Old Norse þéttr.

parole.significato: in, at [with locative] (to express static position/location; the following word starts with a consonant)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic въ (vŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vъ(n), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥, zero-grade form of *h₁én.

parole.significato: to hit, to strike, to smite (to deal a blow)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian уда́рити, вда́рити (udáriti, vdáriti), from Old East Slavic оударити (udariti), from Proto-Slavic *udariti, from Proto-Indo-European *derH-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xovati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъto, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷos-tod, (compare *kʷís).
From Proto-Slavic *květъ, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwoyt-o- (“white, light”).

parole.significato: across, over (from one side to the other of)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic чересъ (čeresŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čersъ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kert-, from *(s)ker-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čekati (“to wait, await, expect”).
From Proto-Slavic *čьrvь, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷr̥mis (“worm”).

parole.significato: across, over (from one side to the other of)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic чересъ (čeresŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čersъ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kert-, from *(s)ker-.

parole.significato: to scoop, to ladle, to bucket, to draw, to spoon (to extract: liquid)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic чьрпати (čĭrpati), from Proto-Slavic *čьrpati, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerp-.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian чи (či), from Old East Slavic чи (či), from Proto-Slavic *či, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷíh₁, initially instrumental singular of pronoun *kʷo-/*kʷe-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *činъ.
From Proto-Slavic *četyre, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.
From Old East Slavic чути (čuti), from Proto-Slavic *čuti, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to perceive”), whence English show and caution. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian чути.
From Proto-Slavic *šestь, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šiti, from Proto-Indo-European *syewH-.
From Proto-Slavic *čьtyre, reduced form of Proto-Slavic *četyre, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šulьga (“someone with their right hand chopped off; leftie”) from Proto-Indo-European *kseul, *kseoul from Proto-Indo-European *kes-, *kos-, *ks-.
From Proto-Slavic *šestь, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.
From Proto-Slavic *(j)ešče (“still, yet”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁esk(ʷ)e(h₁). Cognate with Russian ещё (ješčó).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščebьňь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scratch”).
From Proto-Slavic *čьto, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, *kʷís.
From older form яз (jaz), язъ (jaz), from Old East Slavic ꙗзъ (jazŭ), from Proto-Slavic *(j)azъ. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *éǵh₂.
Inherited from Old East Slavic агнѧ (agnę), ꙗгнѧ (jagnę), from Proto-Slavic *agnę, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷnós.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ѧзы́къ (jazýk), from Old East Slavic ѧзꙑкъ (językŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ęzykъ, from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s.
From Proto-Slavic *jalovъ (“infertile”), from Proto-Indo-European *jal- (“bad”).

parole.significato: ash, ash tree (tree of the genus Fraxinus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *àsenь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *asenь.

From Middle Ukrainian и (y), from Proto-Slavic *i, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ey, an early locative singular determiner, formed from the root *h₁e-, *h₁o-. Compare Ancient Greek εἰ (ei, “if”), Gothic 𐌴𐌹 (ei, “and, so that, be it”).

parole.significato: izgoi (in Kievan Rus, an individual excluded from a particular social status)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic изгои (izgoi) or изгой (izgoj). By surface analysis, із- (iz-) + го́їти (hójity), from Proto-Slavic *gojiti (“to heal, feed”), the latter derived from a causative form of Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃- (“to live”) (whence жи́ти (žýty)).
From Proto-Slavic *mьgla, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃migʰleh₂ (“mist, cloud”). Cognate with Russian мгла (mgla).
From Old East Slavic ити (iti), from Proto-Slavic *jьti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éyti.

Voiced from earlier ки́кнути (kýknuty), from кик (kyk, “death (vulgar)”) + -нути (-nuty), from Proto-Slavic *kykъ (“crook, a certain crooked thing; death (figuratively, taboo)”), from Proto-Indo-European *kew- (“to bend, to crook”), extended to *kew-k. For the semantic development of "crook → death"

parole.significato: lump (a nodule of tissue under the skin as a result of injury)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *gulja from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“"to bend, to curve"”). Related to Polish kula (“ball”) and Ukrainian ку́ля (kúlja, “ball, sphere”).
